title: Commentary: Are Latter-day Saints heeding their prophets’ call and leading out against racism?
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Commentary: Are Latter-day Saints heeding their prophets’ call and leading out against racism?

Latter-day Saints have been directed to their top leaders to "lead out in abandoning attitudes and actions of prejudice.” Are they doing so? Despite some progress on the issue, a religion scholar has his doubts.

Actual Article Body:
(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) Missionaries from the Ghana Missionary Training Center gather to hear apostle Quentin L. Cook speak in early 2026.

Comment

Add as Preferred Source

In 2020, church President Russell M. Nelson pleaded with Latter-day Saints to “do whatever we can” to “preserve the dignity and respect every son and daughter of God deserves” and to “work tirelessly to build bridges of understanding rather than creating walls of segregation.”

Later that same year, he went further: “I call upon our members everywhere to lead out in abandoning attitudes and actions of prejudice.”

(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints via AP) Church President Russell Nelson denounces racism in a 2020 General Conference address.

These statements were part of a larger pattern. In 2018, the church celebrated the 40th anniversary of the revelation that ended the faith’s priesthood and temple ban for Black members. There, President Dallin H. Oaks taught that the lesson of the revelation was a “divine call to abandon attitudes of prejudice against any group of God’s children.”

(Screengrab from BYUtv) Dallin H. Oaks affirmed that Black lives matter in a speech at BYU in October 2020.

Just a year before that, church leadership issued a public statement against white nationalists, affirming that “white supremacist attitudes are morally wrong and sinful, and we condemn them. Church members who promote or pursue a ‘white culture’ or white supremacy agenda are not in harmony with the teachings of the church.”

As recently as 2025, the church created a new webpage, “Race and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints,” that forthrightly denounces white supremacy and racism, while addressing past racism in the church and more.

This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

For many observers of Latter-day Saint culture, these were welcome developments. But six years after Nelson’s exhortation, can we say that Latter-day Saints are “leading out” in the “divine call” to overcome racism and other prejudices?

Latter-day Saints in the United States are diversifying but remain far whiter than the overall population. Fortunately, they are the least likely of any Christian group (7%) to believe that racial diversity weakens American society. They are also the highest Christian group (60%) to report that religious and racial diversity makes America stronger. These numbers were not particularly flattering for Christians — even the relatively high Latter-day Saint numbers were still lower than every other non-Christian religious group’s support of racial and religious diversity.

Why do Latter-day Saints seem to report high approval of racial and religious diversity?

One hypothesis: missions. Tens of thousands of young Latter-day Saints serve volunteer proselytizing stints across the globe every year.

(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) Missionaries are shown in the Philippines. Some believe serving missions helps younger members avoid any attitudes of racism.

Their exposure to diverse cultural, linguistic and national contexts bring higher understanding than their peers. Some older data support this hypothesis for recently returned missionaries, though none shows whether there are longer-term effects.

At the same time, other trends suggest unfinished business in addressing prejudicial attitudes and actions among white American Latter-day Saints. Indeed, I would suggest that many white Latter-day Saints fall into a familiar trend of claiming not to be racist while still exhibiting many behaviors that constitute prejudice.

In recent years, two senior church leaders, general authority Seventy Kyle McKay and Young Men counselor Brad Wilcox, have issued apologies for racist remarks. In another, emeritus general authority Tad Callister wrote approvingly of a “noble sentiment” behind Columbus’ slave trade.
